newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-SOUTH AFRICANS TAKE RACE OUT OF SKIING.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-SOUTH AFRICANS TAKE RACE OUT OF SKIING.

text.p: Like many sports in the time of apartheid, skiing in South Africa was enjoyed only by the white minority but things are beginning to change now -- albeit slowly.

Peter Pilz, coach and manager of South Africa's one-man team at the Alpine skiing world championships, figures it will take five years before one of his class of 10 black skiers graduates to ski racing's big leagues.
Despite the changes in the political climate, the sport remains the winter pursuit of the privileged and wealthy, with most blacks unable to afford expensive equipment, lessons and lift passes.

But South Africa's future World Cup racers may not come from the users of the country's only commercial ski resort in Tiffindel but from the black course workers, who are giving up their lunch hours and spare time to learn about ski racing first-hand.

"We're trying to get workers and their family members who live near the ski resort to get involved in the sport," said Pilz. "We've offered free training and free equipment to the more promising people.
"Right now our training group has about 10 black kids and most of them are very young.
"With the climate in our country, it is now our moral obligation to try and get black skiers involved.
"I think it will still be four or five years until you see a black South African skier on the Europa Cup or World Cup circuit."
Until then, Alexander Heath will continue to carry the South African flag at international ski events -- if allowed.

The 18-year-old Heath is scheduled to race in next week's giant slalom at the world championships but has been barred from taking part in Saturday's downhill by the International Ski Federation (FIS) which feels the Kandahar Banchetta course is too dangerous for the less-experienced racers.
"We want to do the downhill but they (FIS) don't want the smaller nations to participate in speed events," said Pilz. "The responsibility should be with the teams and the team captains.

Heath, who learned to ski on artificial slopes when his parents moved from South Africa to England, raced at last year's championships in Sierra Nevada, Spain, finishing 30th in the giant slalom, 68th in the super-G and 72nd in the downhill.

Although their results place them among ski racings oddities, Pilz resents being bunched with countries such as Algeria, Brazil and Mexico whose commitment to the sport is viewed as less than serious.

Pilz points out that Heath is not a thrill-seeker but a top-ranked junior, who attends the well-respected Waterville Ski Academy in the United States and will compete on the Nor Am circuit, one of the top development leagues for young skiers, next season.
"In South Africa the facilities are not yet there to develop highly competitive skiing," said Pilz. "Eventually you have to go outside to the United States or Europe.
"Our job now is to find and develop the skiers who can compete there."
